dealAnnounced: July 2013 (Saint Thomas Sports Park naming); partnership ended March 1, 2026 when Ascension ended the relationship; replaced by Vanderbilt Health

financials.source: Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements Q4 FY2025; Ascension Q4 FY25 news release September 2025; FierceHealthcare; Becker's Hospital Review. Non-operating revenue derived from reported net income of $918M minus operating loss of -$491M. Figures are for consolidated Ascension system (Ascension Health Alliance, EIN 45-3358926). Same health system as Indianapolis Colts dossier.

balanceSheetWealth.investmentPortfolioSource: Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements Q4 FY2025 — long-term investments of $19,449,512 thousand as of June 30, 2025; plus short-term investments of $43,974 thousand
balanceSheetWealth.notes: Substantially all cash and investments are managed by Ascension Investment Management (AIM), a wholly owned subsidiary. More than $1B allocated to alternative investments including private equity and private credit. As of December 31, 2024 (mid-year FY2025), net unrestricted cash and investments were $15B. System had 228 days cash on hand as of June 30, 2025. Ascension manages assets using an endowment-style approach. Ascension Saint Thomas operates 11 hospital campuses in Tennessee across a 45-county area.

bondDebt.largestIssueProceeds: $2.5 billion — issued through authorities in Indiana, Tennessee, and Texas for capital projects and refunding of previously issued tax-exempt bonds; separate $2.1B taxable bond issuance in November 2025 used to defease remaining tax-exempt subordinate bonds
bondDebt.issuerAuthority: Multiple state health facility finance authorities (Indiana, Tennessee, Texas)
bondDebt.source: Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements Q3 FY2025 ($5.6B long-term debt as of March 31, 2025); Fitch Ratings September 2025 (downgrade affected $5.5B in bonds); Bond Buyer; Fitch expects Ascension to issue up to $4.2B in additional debt. Tennessee is one of the issuing states for Ascension's tax-exempt revenue bonds.

relatedOrganizations.source: Schedule R; Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements; Ascension corporate website; Missouri subsidiary list includes 40+ entities. Same parent system as Indianapolis Colts dossier.

executiveComp.source: Form 990 FY2023 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer and Paddock Post (EIN 45-3358926). Other top executives FY2023: Craig Cordola (EVP/COO) $5,304,408; Eduardo Conrado (Former Board Member) $5,073,352; Elizabeth Foshage (EVP/CFO) $3,981,721; Karen Springer (EVP/CNE) $3,921,283. FY2024 filing shows CEO reportable compensation of $9,963,725 plus $2,317,426 in other compensation ($12,281,151 total). Five-year CEO total (FY2020-2024): approximately $48M.

communityBenefit.source: Ascension community benefit webpage and Ascension Consolidated Financial Statements FY2024. $2.1B in Care of Persons Living in Poverty and Other Community Benefit Programs for FY2024 (ended June 30, 2024). With unpaid costs of Medicare included, total reaches $4.3B. Ascension claims this is four times what it would have paid in taxes as a for-profit company. Percentage calculated against FY2024 total operating revenue of $28.55B. System-wide figure; Ascension Saint Thomas reported $154M in Tennessee community benefit in FY2021 but current Tennessee-specific figure not verified.

taxAdvantage.notes: Ascension claims its $2.1B community benefit is four times what it would have paid in taxes as a for-profit company, implying estimated annual tax advantage of approximately $525M. Operates across 15 states and the District of Columbia with significant tax-exempt property holdings. Tennessee has no state income tax on wages. Ascension Saint Thomas operates 11 hospital campuses across Tennessee, all property-tax-exempt. Tennessee is one of the issuing states for Ascension's tax-exempt revenue bonds.

layoffs.notes: Ascension confirmed layoffs of employees in Texas; primarily nonclinical support roles; declined to specify number of positions affected

Layoffs and hiring freeze triggered by May 2024 ransomware cyberattack and resulting $1.8B operating loss; number unspecified; New York Times alleged system-wide staffing crisis leading to complaints about possible preventable deaths. No Tennessee-specific WARN notices found for Ascension in 2024.
layoffs.source: FierceHealthcare; Becker's Hospital Review; New York Times; Tennessee WARN notice tracker

layoffs.notes: Approximately 500 employees laid off system-wide with reports suggesting total could climb to 1,000; affected locations include Michigan (Ascension St. John), Illinois, Kansas, and Oklahoma. No Tennessee-specific layoffs confirmed in search results.
layoffs.source: Crain's Detroit Business; FierceHealthcare; Lime Entrepreneur

facilityClosures.source: Becker's Hospital Review; FierceHealthcare; Becker's ASC Review

keyRiskFactors: Persistent operating losses — $1.8B loss in FY2024, $491M loss in FY2025, $120M loss through FY2026 Q3
Massive hospital divestiture program reducing portfolio from 139 to 90 facilities since 2022
May 2024 ransomware attack exposing 5.4M patient records and contributing to $1.3B in financial impact
Fitch expects up to $4.2B in additional debt issuance, constraining cash-to-debt ratio
Fitch downgraded from AA+ to AA in September 2025 citing inadequate profitability

program340B.notes: Ascension Rx (Michigan-based Ascension pharmacy subsidiary) previously held contract pharmacy arrangements with Tennessee 340B entities but some were terminated. Pharmaceutical companies have imposed restrictions forcing Ascension hospitals to choose one contract pharmacy within a defined radius; many specialty pharmacies fall outside the typical 40-mile limit.

acquisitions.entity: 4 Middle Tennessee hospitals (from Capella Healthcare joint venture)
acquisitions.notes: Acquired full ownership of hospitals in McMinnville, Smithville, Sparta, and Woodbury; previously co-owned with Capella Healthcare; renamed under the Saint Thomas brand
acquisitions.source: Healthcare Finance News; Catholic Health World

acquisitions.notes: Acquired for $3.9B; expanded ambulatory surgery center footprint from 58 to 300+ centers across 34 states; FTC required divestiture of 6 facilities to Optum subsidiary SC Affiliates; establishes Ascension as third-largest ASC platform nationally
acquisitions.source: Becker's Hospital Review; FierceHealthcare; Bloomberg; Bond Buyer

lobbying.source: OpenSecrets via JAMA Health Forum study (2026); Ascension spent $2.16M on federal lobbying in 2024, ranking among the top health system lobbying spenders alongside Advocate ($2.42M) and Tenet ($2.2M)

legalIssues.description: Ransomware cyberattack compromised personal and health information of 5.4 million individuals; forced electronic health records offline across 19 states including Tennessee; facilities diverted emergency cases to nearby hospitals; class action lawsuit filed alleging failure to implement essential security measures; plaintiffs allege imminent risk of identity theft, fraudulent charges, delayed care, and protected health information posted to dark web
legalIssues.status: Lawsuit moving forward as of October 2025; one of the largest healthcare data breaches in U.S. history
legalIssues.source: HealthExec; Healthcare Dive; CBS News Detroit; Class Law Group

ratios.investmentsToOperatingIncomeInterpretati: Ratio undefined — Ascension reported a $491M operating loss in FY2025. However, the system holds $19.4B in long-term investments (39.6x the magnitude of the operating loss), indicating massive accumulated wealth persisting through sustained operating losses.
ratios.bondDebtToCommunityBenefitInterpretation: Ascension carries $2.67 in tax-exempt bond debt for every $1 it claims in community benefit ($5.6B debt vs $2.1B community benefit)
ratios.charityCareVsStateInterpretation: State average not verified; charity care component of Ascension's $2.1B total community benefit not separately available from search results

accusation: Ascension held $19.4 billion in long-term investments atop $39.9 billion in total assets while posting a $491 million operating loss in FY2025, carrying $5.6 billion in tax-exempt bond debt issued in part through Tennessee authorities, paying its CEO $9.1 million, divesting nearly 50 hospitals, cutting hundreds of jobs, and suffering a ransomware attack that exposed 5.4 million patient records including those at Ascension Saint Thomas facilities in Nashville -- yet spent years as the Tennessee Titans' official healthcare partner with naming rights on the team's training facility (Ascension Saint Thomas Sports Park) before Ascension itself ended the relationship effective March 1, 2026, all while claiming just $2.1 billion in community benefit system-wide on $25.3 billion in revenue and operating 11 tax-exempt hospital campuses across Tennessee.
